title: Identity-Based Revocable and Linkable Ring Signature
abstract:
Revocable and linkable ring signatures ($\mathsf{RLRS}$) provide a practical mechanism for controllable anonymity, enabling a revocation authority (RA) to mandatorily revoke the anonymity of the real signer. However, existing constructions often rely on the assumption of a fully trusted RA, where the correctness of the revocation is not publicly verifiable rendering honest users vulnerable to undetected framing by a compromised RA. Furthermore, the concrete deployment of these schemes is hindered by the certificate management burden of PKI and computation or communication overheads that scale linearly with the ring size, limiting their real-world applicability.
In this paper, we formalize the notion of Identity-Based Revocable and Linkable Ring Signatures ($\mathsf{IB\text{-}RLRS}$), inherently eliminating cumbersome PKI management. Our primary contribution is the enhancement of \textit{revocability} alongside a newly adapted property termed \textit{revocation soundness}, guaranteeing that the real signer's identity can always be extracted, and that a malicious RA cannot frame honest users who did not participate in the signature generation. We present an efficient instantiation of $\mathsf{IB\text{-}RLRS}$ scheme, and prove its security in the random oracle model. Specifically, a novel ring signature construction is proposed, which features a transparent setup and achieves a logarithmic signature size, demonstrating its feasibility for large-scale, privacy-preserving applications.

1   Introduction
Introduced by Rivest et al. [19], ring signatures extend the functionality of stan-
dard digital signatures by enabling signer anonymity. A user can spontaneously
form a set of public keys and produce a signature, while the actual signer remains
hidden within that set. Compared with group signatures [9], ring signatures do
not require any group manager or setup phase, making them particularly suitable
for ad-hoc and decentralized environments.
    While widely deployed in privacy-preserving applications such as e-voting
and conﬁdential transactions, classical ring signatures provide unconditional
anonymity, meaning that the real signer cannot be identiﬁed once the signature

is produced. This limitation can be exploited maliciously, motivating the study
of enhanced variants with controllable anonymity [16, 11, 15, 4, 22, 17]. Recently,
Zhang et al. [24] formalized the notion of RLRS. Their framework enables a RA
to mandatorily revoke the anonymity of a signature in constant time. Simulta-
neously, it allows anyone to publicly link signatures produced by the same signer
under the same event to prevent double spending. To demonstrate its practical
applicability in privacy enhancing technologies, they further extended the RLRS
scheme into a revocable ring conﬁdential transaction protocol, facilitating the
construction of blockchain systems that comply with regulatory requirements.

1.1   Related Work
The development of the RLRS framework builds upon a series of enhancements
designed to achieve controllable anonymity. Initially, Liu et al. [16] proposed
the linkable ring signature (LRS) to detect double spending. To provide fur-
ther regulation, Fujisaki and Suzuki [11] introduced traceable ring signatures,
which reveal the signer’s identity only if they endorse diﬀerent messages. As
this conditional traceability falls short for on-demand revocation, Liu et al. [15]
proposed revocable ring signatures, designating revokers to extract the signer’s
identity. Bootle et al. [4] later formalized accountable ring signatures to allow an
independent opener to extract identities and provide correctness proofs, though
their scheme inherently requires unlinkability. To mitigate centralized regulatory
power, Zhaolu et al. [25] introduced controllable linkable ring signatures to sep-
arate privileges. These foundational works culminated in the RLRS framework,
with recent optimizations like [14] further enhancing performance.
    Limitations of Existing RLRS Schemes. Despite providing controllable
anonymity, the real-world deployment of existing RLRS schemes remains con-
strained by restrictive security models and inherent certiﬁcate management over-
head of PKI. On the one hand, standard revocability deﬁnitions limit the ad-
versary’s corruption capability, failing to capture real-world collusion attacks.
Furthermore, these models implicitly assume a fully trusted RA, rendering the
revocation process publicly unveriﬁable and leaving honest users vulnerable to
undetected framing. On the other hand, most RLRS schemes are conﬁned to the
traditional PKI setting. The immense certiﬁcate management overhead makes
them unsuitable for highly scalable and decentralized environments.
    The Quest for Eﬃcient Identity-Based RLRS. Identity-based cryptog-
raphy [20] oﬀers an alternative to eliminate the PKI burden. However, migrating
ring signatures to the ID-based setting introduces an inherent trade-oﬀ between
signature size and transparent setup. Early IBRS constructions (e.g., [23, 5])
feature concise setups but exhibit computational and communication overheads
that scale linearly with the ring size. Accumulator-based schemes [18] success-
fully compress signatures to a constant size, but at the expense of introducing a
trapdoor key escrow vulnerability. Recently, building on the techniques of [12],
Nassurdine et al. [17] proposed a transparent ID-based linkable ring signature
scheme with logarithmic size. Nevertheless, this approach relies on complex un-
derlying zero-knowledge proofs, incurring heavy computational complexity. This

stands in contrast to the PKI setting, where numerous eﬃcient logarithmic-size
ring signature schemes have been proposed [22, 13, 3].

1.2    Our Contributions
The main contributions of this work are summa- rized as follows:
 1. Formalization of the IB-RLRS. We formalize the notion of Identity-Based
    Revocable and Linkable Ring Signatures (IB-RLRS). We strengthen revoca-
    bility to guarantee that the actual signer’s identity can always be extracted
    by the RA, even under the full compromise of all ring keys. Furthermore,
    we introduce revocation soundness, a notion adapted from accountable ring
    signatures, to ensure that even a fully corrupted RA cannot frame an honest
    user who did not participate in the signature generation.
 2. Construction with Transparent Setup. We present an eﬃcient construc-
    tion of the IB-RLRS, denoted BLMQ-RLRS, together with a formal security
    analysis in the random oracle model. Our construction integrates the BLMQ
    signature scheme [1], the set membership proof [22], and the Twisted ElGa-
    mal encryption [10]. Our novel construction achieves logarithmic signature
    size without requiring trusted setup in the ID-based setting.

3      Identity-Based Revocable and Linkable Ring Signature

In this section we formalize the syntax of identity-based revocable and linkable
ring signature(IB-RLRS), and deﬁne its security model.


3.1      Syntax

An IB-RLRS scheme involves four entities: the KGC, the RA, the signer and the
veriﬁer, and it consists of eight algorithms (Setup, RevokeKeyGen, KeyExt, Sign,
Verify, Link, Revoke, Judge).

    – (pp, msk) ← Setup(λ): On input a security parameter λ, the KGC generates
      and publishes the public parameters pp, while secretly retaining the master
      secret key msk. Assume pp is implicitly provided to all subsequent algorithms.
    – (pkR , skR ) ← RevokeKeyGen(pp): The RA generates the keypair (pkR , skR ),
      used to trace the actual signer during disputes.
    – dID ← KeyExt(msk, ID): The KGC takes as input the msk and an identity
      ID ∈ {0, 1}∗ , outputs the private key dID associated with the identity ID.
    – σ ← Sign(event, pkR , dID , L, m): The signer takes as input the event, the RA’s
      public key pkR , its private key dID , a ring L of identities with ID ∈ L, and a
      message m, outputs a signature σ.
    – {0, 1} ← Verify(event, pkR , L, m, σ): The veriﬁer takes as input the event,
      the RA’s public key pkR , the ring L, the message m and the signature σ. It
      outputs 1 if σ is valid, and 0 otherwise.
    – {0, 1}/⊥ ← Link(event, pkR1 , pkR2 , L1 , L2 , m1 , m2 , σ1 , σ2 ): On input two tu-
      ples (Li , mi , σi , pkRi ), i ∈ {0, 1} and the event, outputs ⊥ if either signature
      is invalid. Otherwise, outputs 1 if the signatures are linked, and 0 otherwise.
    – (ID, π) / ⊥ ← Revoke(event, skR , L, m, σ): The RA takes as input a tuple
      (L, m, σ) under the event, and its private key skR , outputs ⊥ if the signature
      is invalid. Otherwise, outputs the real identity ID ∈ L of the signer together
      with a zero-knowledge proof π.

4      Eﬃcient Construction with Logarithmic Signature Size
4.1      Technical Overview
We present a concrete instantiation of our scheme, named BLMQ-RLRS, by in-
tegrating the IEEE P1363 signature scheme, Bulletproofs membership proof,
Twisted ElGamal public-key encryption, and Chaum-Pedersen protocol as the
core building blocks. Our proposed scheme is motivated from [18, 4, 22].
    Let L = {ID1 , . . . , IDn } be the ring of identities, and let the signer’s identity
be IDπ , π ∈ [n]. To generate a ring signature, the signer must prove that (i)The
signer holds a valid private key dIDπ issued by the KGC, and (ii) IDπ ∈ L.
To do so, the signer compute the commitment c = Com(xπ ; rc ) of her identity

A.3   Signatures of Knowledge
Let R be a polynomial time recognizable relation and LR := {s | ∃w, s.t.(s, w) ∈
R} denote the language associated with R. A signature of knowledge scheme SoK
for the relation R typically consists of the following PPT algorithms:
 – Setup(λ) → pp: It takes as input the security parameter λ and outputs the
   public parameters pp, which implicitly deﬁne a relation R.
 – Sign(s, w, m) → σ: It takes as input a statement s, a witness w, and a
   message m ∈ {0, 1}∗ and outputs a signature of knowledge σ on m.
 – Verify(s, m, σ) → {0, 1}: It takes as input a statement s, a message m, and
   a signature σ, and outputs 1 if the signature is valid and 0 otherwise.
   A signature of knowledge scheme should be simulatable and extractable.
